data.name: Poltergeist: A Pixelated Horror
data.detailed_description:
Have you ever wondered what it feels to be a ghostly being?

You have always lived happily in your mansion. A mansion that you managed to obtain with a lot of hard work and many personal sacrifices. Naturally you don't want anyone else to take care of it, not even in death! But now, after your demise, many tenants have taken over it, and this is intolerable to you.
Luckily, your love for your manor has granted you powers that will help you get rid of those pesky individuals.

Watch them run and scream, scaring them using your intelligence, wit, and with the use of powers like possessions, spectres, altering objects and more.
Have fun and play with the occult... and become a Poltergeist!

Poltergeist: A Pixelated Horror is a puzzle game for PC/Mac/Linux, in which you are a ghost named Henry B. Knight. You will scare the tenants currently living in your house, so you can have some peace at last in the afterlife.

reviews.review:
Ghost Master was the ultimate ghost game back in the year 2003 when it was first released. The ability to play as a ghost where you had to scare away people was a fun and unique experience, but somehow the idea hasn’t been used in many other games after that one. The ones that did use it usually failed or were just mildly successful. So will Poltergeist A Pixelated Horror succeed where others have failed ? Let’s take a closer look.

Poltergeist A Pixelated Horror (from now on referenced as Poltergeist if necessary) is at its heart a puzzle game and not a ‘real’ ghost simulator. You can’t use your tricks and summons infinitely, there’s a limit to how many times you can perform a certain action. But before I get to this I’ll try to tell you a little bit more about the game itself.
After having lived in a mansion his entire life, Henry B. Knight (the main character of the game) eventually dies. Naturally, new people will start living in this mansion, but you can’t and won’t accept this. In fact, you won’t be able to find peace until you’ve scared them all away. So it’s here that your quest to retake the mansion begins. 
As you can clearly see Henry B. Knight is the star of the game. But you won’t actually see him all that often. He’ll sometimes appear as a ‘special power’ ghost to scare away bosses, but other than that (and for some small cutscenes) you will hardly ever see him. This is weird but also acceptable since the game is played from an isometric perspective, also known as a bird’s-eye view.
Each level has a couple of rooms tied together. In each room there’s usually at least one person or animal to be found, as well as some objects like TV’s, beds and chairs. The exit can be located anywhere, it doesn’t really matter, because once a person or animal is spooked he, she or it will automatically find their way towards this exit. The one thing you have to think about it is how to use the tools you’re given to scare everyone away. Some of the levels will be easy and some of the later levels will absolutely challenge your mind. But fortunately you can always restart a level if things don’t entirely go your way.
Each inhabitant has a meter that shows how easily one is spooked. A full meter (three circles) seems to be the limit but there’s also the possibility that a meter is black. This means you have to scare the person first before you’re able to see how full their meter actually is.
There are quite a few ways to scare people; you have the basic tricks like moving objects and making noise or you can sometimes summon a ghost or a ghost that can take over people and walk around.
I’ve mentioned it before already, but since this is a puzzle game your objective is to use all of your available tools (or less, of course) to empty the rooms. Sometimes special characters (like exorcists and ghost hunters) will appear and these people have the ability to block one or more of your powers. In the beginning this is sometimes annoying, because if an action is blocked or stopped this means you usually have to restart the level. Later levels will allow you to finish it without having to use up all of your powers (if you play it strategically) making it a little bit more open and accessible. 
There’s no hint system so you have to figure things out all by yourself. This is sometimes a little harder than expected; I’ve played early levels that took me more than a few tries while I could finish other, later levels in one go.
Poltergeist uses multiple settings like the traditional (1800/1900’s) mansion but there’s also a modern setting and even an office to haunt. In total there are 60 levels; 15 for each setting with the last three levels being boss encounters. I’m not sure why there are even boss encounters;  the idea sounds cool, but the execution is very poor. That’s because the boss fight levels are essentially the same as all the other levels, but the deal here is that the boss can only be scared away once all other inhabitants are gone. After that you can summon the ghost of Henry to scare him off. This last part is done with a simple mouseclick and there’s no real interaction. I think this could’ve used a little more thought. But other than that this is good fun.

Poltergeist isn’t outstanding in its graphics department. In fact, its style is a bit of a coherent mess. I understand that it’s probably because of financial and/or time constraints, but it uses both 2D sprites and 3D models. The sprites are okay but charmingly animated, but once the 3D models start to appear you get thrown out of the experience because – to me – it just doesn’t look right. Or the other way around, I’m not sure. The textures on the other hand are very well done.
The interface is basic but gets the job done. A little more polish, a bit of resizing and maybe some extra color would’ve been nice but it’s good enough to understand what each icon does.
The music is perfect with haunting, Exorcist-like tunes. It’s done very well and complements the atmosphere, even though the game isn’t about scary or creepy stuff (the setting, however, is). The frightened people, as well as their screams when they are running away, are realistic and believable. There’s also nothing wrong with the sound effects; they might feel unnecessary at first but they’re essential to let the gamers know that something is actually happening. So every object and summon you use will make a sound.

Length wise there’s more than enough gameplay to keep you occupied for at least several hours. Each of the levels takes but a few minutes (if you know exactly what to do) so getting through the 60 levels will take you anywhere between 4-7 hours I think. I can’t complain here, there’s more than enough to do.

Poltergeist might not become a classic like Ghost Master but despite that it has become an entertaining puzzle game worthy of my time. It doesn’t bring anything new to the table but anyone looking for another ghost game, or just a good puzzle game in general, will absolutely have fun with this.
